title: Turkey's parliament approves conditional pardon for PKK militants contingent on full disarmament
dek: Turkey's parliament voted 468-88 on Monday to approve legislation offering a conditional pardon to thousands of Kurdish PKK insurgents, with the pardon taking effect only after the group fully disarms and dissolves. The PKK announced last year it was ending its armed campaign in response to a call from imprisoned leader Abdullah Ocalan. The measure offers political advantage to President Erdogan by potentially securing support from pro-Kurdish lawmakers.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Turkey's parliament voted 468-88 to approve legislation introducing a conditional pardon for thousands of PKK militants, contingent on verified disarmament and group dissolution.
bottom_line: The pardon remains conditional on verified disarmament overseen by Turkey's National Security Council, a requirement that will determine whether the PKK follows through on its announced dissolution. The group's public insistence on Ocalan's release and expanded political freedoms, combined with its criticism of the bill's shortcomings, signals potential friction points ahead even as the legislative framework is now in place.
body: Turkey's parliament voted 468-88 on Monday to approve legislation introducing a conditional pardon for thousands of Kurdish PKK militants, marking a major shift in the country's approach to a conflict that has killed tens of thousands of people since 1984.

The pardon will take effect only after Turkish authorities verify that the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK, has fully disarmed and dissolved, according to NPR's reporting. The group announced last year that it was ending its decades-long armed campaign against the Turkish state in response to a call from its imprisoned leader, Abdullah Ocalan. The PKK staged a symbolic disarmament ceremony in northern Iraq, where it is based, and announced it was withdrawing fighters from key locations in Turkey to Iraq.

The 12-article legislation outlines procedures for the group's disarmament and the rehabilitation of thousands of PKK members. According to NPR, the law will suspend some prison sentences for convicted PKK members and postpone ongoing investigations and trials against others for five or 10 years depending on the severity of alleged offenses. If no terror-related crime is committed within the time frame, the cases will be dropped. However, militants convicted of intentional killings and those sentenced to life terms before 2005 are excluded from the bill's provisions, as is Ocalan and other senior PKK figures.

The measures will come into effect only after Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the group has disbanded and surrendered all weapons, per NPR's reporting. Those seeking to benefit from the law will have six months to apply after the National Security Council's decision is published in the official gazette. Media reports have said exiled PKK members and those in Iraq and Syria are expected to benefit.

Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus told reporters following the vote: "With the armed organization laying down its arms and dissolving itself, we will build a new era in which peace, brotherhood, and solidarity will prevail." Gulistan Kilic Kocyigit of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party, or DEM, told parliament: "The people of Turkey, who have paid a heavy price for many years, now have an opportunity to consolidate peace and build democracy," while acknowledging the proposal has shortcomings.

The PKK, however, offered a mixed response. According to NPR, the PKK-linked ANF news outlet carried a statement from the group describing the legislation as a "beginning" to resolving outstanding issues but containing "serious shortcomings and deficiencies." The PKK called for Ocalan's release from prison, saying the peace process can move forward only if he "lives and works freely." The group also said that fighters would not surrender weapons and return to Turkey "if, upon returning to Turkey, they are unable to engage in democratic politics on the basis of freedom of thought and freedom of association, and if they are prosecuted and imprisoned because of their views or the organizations they establish." The PKK said the legislation failed to address demands for democratic reforms and Kurdish rights.

The measure also carries political dimensions beyond the conflict itself. According to NPR, the legislation offers Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan the opportunity to court the support of the pro-Kurdish DEM party to help him remain in office beyond the presidential two-term limit, which Erdogan could exceed if parliament calls an early election during his current term. The center-right nationalist Good Party, which opposed the bill, argued it "would pave the way" for Erdogan to stay in power. DEM has previously lobbied for Ocalan, imprisoned since 1999, to be granted official status to coordinate the transition process, potentially leading to his release, but the current proposal makes no mention of his status or possible release. Media reports have suggested that Ocalan's conditions in his island prison off Istanbul will likely be improved.

The measure also sets broader geopolitical implications. According to NPR, the decision to disarm could lead to closer Turkish-Iraqi ties and may support the Syrian government's efforts to integrate areas that were under the control of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, affiliated with the PKK. The PKK has been designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States, and the European Union. The group initially sought an independent Kurdish state but later shifted to demands for autonomy and expanded rights in Turkey. Previous peace efforts between Turkey and the PKK have failed, most recently in 2015.
